title: PROGRAMMING PARADIGMS
body:
A functional programming course, taught in [[Haskell]], with [[Lambda Calculus]] as the formal
spine and [[Category Theory]] arriving through [[Monad|monads]]. The framing is comparative,
because you cannot see what a paradigm decided until you have seen the alternatives, and by
third year you have written four languages in three other paradigms: [[C]] in
[[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]], [[Java]] in [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]], [[Assembly]] in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY]], [[JavaScript]] in [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]]. Every one of them was
imperative underneath. This course takes the mutable variable away and asks what is left.

The punchline is settled before the course starts, by [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]]: every
one of these models computes exactly the same set of functions. So a paradigm is never about
power. It is about what you can say briefly, what the compiler can check for you, and which
class of bug you stop being able to write. The functional answer to that last question is
specific and aggressive: **remove mutable state, and an entire category of bug becomes
unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged.**

## Topics

### The word means two things

[[Paradigms]] · [[Design]] · [[Structured Approach]] · [[Object Oriented Approach]]

[[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] has a note called [[Paradigms]] and it means something
narrower: **design** paradigms, how to decompose a system, [[Structured Approach]] (split by
function) against [[Object Oriented Approach]] (split by thing). This course means **language**
paradigms, what a program is built out of. Different axes, and they come apart: you can write
OO designs in C with structs and function pointers, and plenty of Java is structured code with a
class wrapped round it because the language demanded one.

### The four models side by side

The comparison the course hangs off, and no other note in the vault holds it. Read the
Functional column as the subject and the other three as the contrast:

| | Imperative / procedural | Object oriented | **Functional** | Declarative |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A program is | a sequence of commands | objects sending messages | **expressions being evaluated** | a description of the answer |
| The unit is | the procedure | the [[Classes\|class]] | **the [[Function\|function]]** | the rule or the query |
| State | global and mutable | partitioned, owned by an object | **avoided; values replace variables** | not exposed at all |
| Repetition by | the loop | the loop | **[[Recursion Schemes\|recursion]]** | recursion or set operations |
| You specify | how | how, in smaller pieces | **what to compute** | what you want, not how |
| Model behind it | [[Turing Machine]] | Turing machine with walls | **[[Lambda Calculus]]** | logic and relations |
| In the vault | [[C]], [[Assembly]] | [[Java]], [[Classes]] | **[[Haskell]], [[Lambda Calculus]]** | [[SQL]], [[React]], [[Regular Expressions]] |

The "State" row is the one that predicts things. Almost every argument between paradigms
reduces to who is allowed to mutate what, and this course takes the position at the far end of
that row. See [[Immutability]].

### Why the choice is expressive, not computational

[[Turing Machine]] · [[Lambda Calculus]] · [[Cellular Automata]] · [[Undecidability]] ·
[[Simulation]]

The two paradigms with a formal ancestor both got one in 1936, independently, answering the
same question:

| Model | Built from | Grew into |
|---|---|---|
| [[Turing Machine]] | a state machine and a mutable tape | imperative and object-oriented languages |
| [[Lambda Calculus]] | functions and substitution, nothing else | Lisp, ML, [[Haskell]], and the functional features in everything else |
| general recursive functions, register machines, [[Cellular Automata]] | various | nothing directly, but they land in the same place |

They compute exactly the same class of functions. That convergence is the evidence for the
Church-Turing thesis, and it is why this course cannot be about capability: anything Turing
complete can [[Simulation|simulate]] anything else Turing complete. [[Undecidability]] applies
to all of them equally; the halting problem is not a bug in imperative programming that Haskell
fixed.

What differs is cost of expression, and [[Lambda Calculus]] makes the point in miniature: no
numbers, no booleans, no loops, and it encodes all of them out of functions. Everything is
*possible*, most of it is *unpleasant*, and that gap is the entire subject. **[[Haskell]] is
that calculus with names, types, and a compiler**, which is the sentence the whole course
elaborates.

### The language

[[Haskell]] · [[Pure Function]] · [[Immutability]]

Three properties, taken together, and the course's argument is that they reinforce each other
rather than merely coexist:

| Property | Note | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure** | [[Pure Function]] | referential transparency; reordering, caching, and parallelism become safe |
| **Lazy** | [[Lazy Evaluation]] | infinite structures, and unpredictable timing |
| **Statically typed** | [[Static Typing]] | effects and absence are visible in signatures |

[[Immutability]] is the data-side statement of the first: names bind once, `x = x + 1` is an
equation with no solution, and updates build new values that share structure with the old ones.
Purity is what makes laziness safe, because evaluation order cannot be observed if nothing
observable happens during evaluation; the type system is what makes purity enforceable rather
than a convention. Take away any one and the other two stop working.

### Functions as the unit

[[Recursion Schemes]] · [[Partial Application]] · [[List Comprehension]] ·
[[Recursive Backtracking]] · [[Recursion]]

With no loop, [[Recursion]] is not a technique, it is the only means of repetition, so
[[Recursion Schemes]] names the shapes it takes: structural recursion (guaranteed to terminate,
and the reason induction applies), accumulator passing, tail recursion, and the folds that
abstract the first two.

[[Partial Application]] is the other half of the model. Every function takes exactly one
argument, so `f x y` is `(f x) y` and supplying too few arguments returns a function rather than
an error. That is currying, straight out of [[Lambda Calculus]], and it is why `map (* 2)` needs
no lambda.

[[List Comprehension]] is set-builder notation from [[Sets]] with brackets, and it turns out to
be the list [[Monad]] wearing different syntax. [[Recursive Backtracking]] is that observation
cashed out: search with generators as choices and guards as pruning, and because nothing is
mutable there is no undo step at all, which is the whole difficulty in the imperative
[[Backtracking]] version.

### Types

[[Static Typing]] · [[Type Inference]] · [[Algebraic Data Type]] · [[Type Class]] ·
[[Parametric Polymorphism]]

One of the two topics the course leans on hardest. [[Static Typing]] means checked before the
program runs, and what makes Haskell's version stronger than [[C]]'s is that **there is no
cast**: C checks types and then lets you [[Type casting|cast]] around the check, so its
guarantee is advisory. [[Type Inference]] (Hindley-Milner) is what makes that affordable, by
finding the most general type of every expression with no annotations required.

[[Algebraic Data Type]] is how you define types: sums (`|`, one of) and products (fields, all
of), taken apart by pattern matching, with the compiler warning on any match you left
incomplete. `Maybe a = Nothing | Just a` is the famous consequence, putting the possibility of
absence *into the type* so that everything else is guaranteed not to be null.

Two kinds of polymorphism, and this is the vault's disambiguation job:
[[Parametric Polymorphism]] is one implementation for every type, which cannot inspect its
values and gets its guarantees from that ignorance, against [[Polymorphism]] (COMP 2633), which
is many implementations dispatched at run time. [[Type Class]] is the third kind, ad-hoc:
different code per type, retrofittable onto types you did not write, and able to dispatch on the
**return** type in a way no [[Interface]] can.

### Evaluation

[[Lazy Evaluation]] · [[Nondeterminism]]

Nothing is computed until demanded. That buys infinite structures (`fibs` defined in terms of
itself, an unbounded prime sieve), lets `head (filter p xs)` stop at the first hit, and makes
`if` and `&&` ordinary functions rather than syntax. It costs space leaks, unpredictable
timing, and cost analysis that depends on the consumer rather than the code.

[[Nondeterminism]] enters from [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] rather than from the language.
Its two readings, guess a branch and explore all branches, are the specification of which the
list [[Monad]] is the implementation, and the [[NFA]]'s accept-if-some-path-accepts is the same
idea one level of abstraction down. Determinism is then a claim about the *program*: a
[[Pure Function]] is deterministic by construction, so nondeterminism in this setting is
something you introduce deliberately, as a data structure, rather than something you fight.

### Structure and proof

[[Functor]] · [[Monad]] · [[Monadic IO]] · [[Category Theory]] · [[Program Correctness]]

The [[Type Class]] ladder [[Functor]] → `Applicative` → [[Monad]] answers three progressively
harder questions about applying a function inside a structure, and only the top rung lets a
later step depend on an earlier step's *value*. [[Monad]] is the hub note: `return` and `>>=`,
the three laws, `do` notation as pure sugar, and the point that `Maybe`, `Either`, lists,
`State`, and `IO` are one interface over unrelated plumbing.

[[Monadic IO]] is how a pure language performs effects. The move is that an `IO a` is a
*description* of an action rather than the action, so building one is pure and only the runtime
executes the one that `main` evaluates to. There is no `IO a -> a`, so a function typed
`Int -> Int` provably did no input or output, which is the strongest single statement the type
system makes.

[[Category Theory]] is where the monad definition comes from, and the course went far enough in
to derive it: objects and arrows, functors preserving identity and composition, natural
transformations, and then a monad as an endofunctor with $\eta$ and $\mu$ satisfying the monoid
axioms. The nicest result along the way is that **naturality is parametricity**: a
`forall a. F a -> G a` cannot inspect its elements, so the commuting square is free.

[[Program Correctness]] is the payoff. Purity makes `=` mean equality, so you may substitute
equals for equals; [[Algebraic Data Type]] hands you the case split; and structural induction is
[[Proof By Induction]] with $\mathbb{N}$ replaced by a recursive type. [[Induction]] in
[[DISCRETE MATH]] predicted this course by name.

### Where you have already seen it

The functional features arrived in the mainstream through JavaScript, so most of this is
recognition rather than novelty:

| Feature | Comes from | Seen in |
|---|---|---|
| functions are values | abstraction $\lambda x. M$ is a term like any other | [[JS Functions]]: functions are [[Objects]] |
| higher-order functions | application $M\ N$ where $M$ is a parameter | [[Call Back Function]], `setTimeout` |
| anonymous functions | lambda terms never needed names | [[Anonymous Function]], [[Arrow Syntax]] |
| closures | a term keeps its free variables bound | [[Closure]], reached from [[Objects]] |
| `map` / `filter` / `reduce` | folds over a structure | [[Array Functions]] |
| currying | one argument at a time | [[Partial Application]], the default in Haskell |
| recursion without a loop | the Y combinator | [[Recursion]], [[Recursion Schemes]] |
| immutable state | values, not variables | [[React]]'s "never mutate state directly" |

The difference is enforcement. JavaScript *offers* these; Haskell gives you no alternative, and
that is what makes the guarantees hold.

### The contrast cases

[[C]] · [[Assembly]] · [[Subroutines]] · [[Stack and Heap]] · [[Object Oriented]] ·
[[Classes]] · [[Encapsulation]] · [[Inheritance]] · [[Polymorphism]] · [[Java]]

**Imperative** is the default that needs no justification, because it is what the hardware does:
a list of commands that change memory, which is [[Instructions|an instruction stream]] with
better names. **Procedural** adds the [[Subroutines|subroutine]] and with it the call stack,
which is where local [[Variable Scope|scope]], automatic lifetimes, and [[Recursion]] come from.
Its failure mode is the one [[Structured Approach]] names: data and the functions over it are
separate, so a change to a structure reaches every function that touches it.

**Object oriented** is not a different computational model; it is imperative programming with
the mutable state fenced off, one [[Object]] at a time, which is [[Encapsulation]]. The
functional answer to the same problem is more radical and is the comparison worth holding:

| | OO answer | Functional answer |
|---|---|---|
| The problem | shared mutable state has unbounded blast radius | same |
| The fix | restrict **who** may mutate | remove **mutation** |
| Enforced by | [[Encapsulation]], access modifiers | the language having no assignment |
| Cost | state still exists, so aliasing and [[Concurrency]] still bite | no in-place update; see [[Immutability]] |

**Declarative** describes the result and lets something else pick the algorithm: [[SQL]]'s
planner chooses the join order, [[React]] diffs rather than being told to mutate the DOM, a
[[Regular Expressions|regex]] describes a set of [[Strings]] and something else builds the
[[NFA]]. Functional programming is adjacent but not the same: a [[List Comprehension]] *is*
declarative, and a fold is not. Logic programming (Prolog) is the fifth paradigm and the vault
has no note on it; its execution model is [[Recursive Backtracking]] plus unification, which is
also the [[Type Inference|unification]] that Hindley-Milner runs over types.

### Concurrency, where the choice stops being taste

[[Concurrency]] · [[Thread]] · [[Shared Memory]] · [[Message Passing]] · [[Synchronization]] ·
[[Mutex Lock]] · [[Spin Lock]] · [[Semaphores]] · [[Critical Section]]

Everything above is arguable until more than one thing runs at once, and then the "State" row
starts costing money. [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] has both halves already:

| Approach | Paradigm | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| [[Shared Memory]] plus locks | imperative, OO | correctness is manual: every [[Critical Section]] needs a [[Mutex Lock]] or a [[Semaphores\|semaphore]], and missing one is a race |
| [[Message Passing]] | actor-style, functional-adjacent | copying, and you design the protocol |
| no shared mutable state at all | functional | you give up in-place update |

A race needs shared data *and* a writer. [[Immutability]] removes the writer, so the race is not
prevented, it is unrepresentable, and every lock note in [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] exists to patch a
problem that immutable values never have. That is the most practical argument the paradigm has,
and it is why [[Pure Function]] and [[Immutability]] are the two Tier 1 notes of the first half.

## Core Facts to Know

- This course is functional programming in [[Haskell]]; the other paradigms are the contrast.
- A paradigm is a model of what a program is made of, not a set of language features.
- Design paradigms and language paradigms are different axes; [[Paradigms]] in COMP 2633 is the first.
- All Turing-complete languages compute the same class of functions, so paradigms differ in expressiveness, never power.
- [[Turing Machine]] (state plus mutable tape) is the ancestor of imperative languages; [[Lambda Calculus]] (functions plus substitution) of functional ones.
- Both were published in 1936, independently: the Church-Turing thesis.
- [[Undecidability]] applies to every paradigm equally.
- [[Haskell]] is [[Lambda Calculus]] with names, types, and a compiler.
- It is pure, lazy, and statically typed, and the three depend on each other.
- A [[Pure Function]] returns the same result for the same arguments and changes nothing else.
- **Referential transparency**: an expression may be replaced by its value, which licenses reordering, caching, and parallelism.
- [[Immutability]]: names bind once; update means building a new value that shares structure.
- With no loop, [[Recursion]] is the only repetition; [[Recursion Schemes]] names its shapes.
- Structural recursion always terminates on finite data, which is what licenses structural induction.
- Every function takes one argument: `f x y` is `(f x) y`. That is currying; see [[Partial Application]].
- [[List Comprehension]] is set-builder notation, and desugars to `map`, `filter`, and `concatMap`.
- [[Lazy Evaluation]]: nothing computes until demanded, so infinite structures are ordinary values.
- Laziness costs space leaks and unpredictable timing, and is safe only because the language is pure.
- [[Static Typing]] means checked before running; Haskell's is strong because there is no cast, unlike [[C]]'s.
- [[Type Inference]] (Hindley-Milner) finds the **principal type**, the most general one.
- [[Algebraic Data Type]]: sums (one of) and products (all of), eliminated by pattern matching.
- Non-exhaustive matches are compiler warnings, so adding a constructor produces a work list.
- `Maybe a = Nothing | Just a` puts absence in the type, so other types cannot be null.
- [[Parametric Polymorphism]] is one implementation for all types; [[Polymorphism]] (COMP 2633) is many, dispatched at run time.
- **Parametricity**: a parametric function cannot inspect its values, so `a -> a` can only be `id`.
- [[Type Class]] is ad-hoc polymorphism: retrofittable, compile-time dispatch, and can dispatch on the return type.
- [[Functor]] → `Applicative` → [[Monad]] is a hierarchy; only [[Monad]] lets a step depend on the previous result.
- A [[Monad]] is `return` plus `>>=`, obeying left identity, right identity, and associativity.
- `do` notation is sugar: `x <- e` is `e >>= \x ->`.
- The list monad's `>>=` is `concatMap`, so it is [[Recursive Backtracking]] and [[Nondeterminism]].
- An `IO a` is a **description** of an effect, not the effect; only the runtime performs it.
- There is no `IO a -> a`, so a signature without `IO` proves the function did no I/O.
- In [[Category Theory]]: a monad is an endofunctor with $\eta$ (`return`) and $\mu$ (`join`) satisfying the monoid axioms.
- `m >>= f = join (fmap f m)`; bind is map-then-flatten.
- Naturality is parametricity: a `forall a. F a -> G a` commutes with `fmap` for free.
- [[Program Correctness]]: equational reasoning plus structural induction, available only because the language is pure.
- Structural induction is [[Proof By Induction]] with $\mathbb{N}$ replaced by a recursive type.
- A race needs shared data and a writer, so [[Immutability]] makes races unrepresentable rather than merely rarer.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613), the theoretical prerequisite and the course
  that points here. [[Lambda Calculus]] is where all of this comes from, [[Turing Machine]] is
  the contrast, and [[Undecidability]] is the shared limit. [[Nondeterminism]] and the [[NFA]]
  are the specification the list [[Monad]] implements.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271): [[Proof By Induction]] and [[Induction]] are half of
  [[Program Correctness]], and [[Sets]] is where [[List Comprehension]]'s notation is from.
- [[ABSTRACT ALGEBRA]] (MATH 2101): [[Group]], [[Homomorphism]], and [[Isomorphism]] are the
  structure-preserving-map habit that [[Category Theory]] generalises, and the monoid axioms are
  the [[Monad]] laws.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633): [[Recursion]] owns what recursion is and
  what a frame costs. [[C]], [[Type casting]], [[Variable]], and [[Structure]] are the
  static-typing and mutable-state contrast throughout.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]] (COMP 2633): the *design* sense of [[Paradigms]], and
  [[Polymorphism]], which shares a word with [[Parametric Polymorphism]] and nothing else.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): [[Java]], and the [[Abstract Data Type]] separation of
  interface from implementation, which [[Type Class]] does differently.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655): [[Assembly]] and [[Subroutines]] are the paradigm
  underneath all the others, and the tail-call story in [[Recursion Schemes]] cashes out there.
- [[WEB DEVELOPMENT FOR CS]] (COMP 3612): [[JS Functions]], [[Closure]], [[Arrow Syntax]],
  [[Array Functions]], and [[React]] are where these features actually got used, and [[Void]] is
  the sharpest anti-example for purity.
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]] (COMP 3659): [[Concurrency]], [[Thread]], [[Shared Memory]],
  [[Message Passing]], and the locks. The practical case against shared mutable state.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]]: [[Recursion]], [[Backtracking]], and [[Dynamic Programming]]
  are where thinking recursively pays off, and [[Time Complexity]] is what
  [[Lazy Evaluation]] complicates.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: [[Simulation]] and [[Chomsky Hierarchy]] for the
  one-machine-imitating-another material.
